doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: First Columbia album: 'S Wonderful and choosing songs by arithmetic
summary: He picks top-ten hits from the years his 18-35 audience fell in love, adds voices by accident, Mitch Miller likes it, and the 'S Wonderful album becomes a gold record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: them — I picked songs, and by arithmetic I went back the number of years, the age group I was trying to hit was 18-35 in the market. So I went back, when were those 18 to 35 year olds hearing, “ooooh would you like to take a walk” with the little girl down the street, or the boy you know, and so by arithmetic I picked songs from the top ten of those years. And that’s what “S’ Wonderful,” “S’ Marvelous,” “S’ Awful Nice.” So in other words I didn’t change my style of writing that much. I still wrote for brass and saxes, big band style, with a predominant rhythm sound, and I added the voices quite accidentally. It was just an experiment on a single I originally was backing for Columbia Records. And Mitch Miller was head of all the artists at Columbia. He came running out and he says, “this is a great sound. We’ve got to get you back in the studio, have you do a couple of sides, Ray Conniff, orchestra and chorus, and use that orchestra and chorus sound.” And so the first thing we did was a single. It was called on one side was “Begin the Beguine,” and I did some more research and found out that the two songs that had sold the most records, had the most sheet music, and playing, the most airplay and it was “Begin the Beguine” and “Stardust.” That was in 1956. And we put the single out. And it became like a turntable hit. It was played day and night by disc jockeys all over the United States. And as a matter of fact, well no it wasn’t until the album — the single, oddly enough, wasn’t selling very much, with saturation airplay. And Columbia Records would have meetings in the marketing. “What is it with this Conniff? We’re not selling his single and that’s all you hear on the air.” And a fellow by the name of Hal Cook in marketing come up with the answer. He says “you know, I think we’re on the wrong track with Ray Conniff. He’s not a single artist. He’s an album artist. Get him back in the studio with ten more songs and put out an album, and I think we’ll have something.” And so that’s what we did. And one of the other ten songs was “S’ Wonderful,” which we decided to use for the title song, and I used that instruments and — voices and instrument sound and the predominant rhythm sound, and the idea about people falling in love to the songs, and then that album, and the title song of that, “S’ Wonderful,” that became a turntable hit. It was on a chart that Billboard magazine had for about, I don’t know, it’s not on any longer, but it was only ten albums would appear on that chart, and the chart said, “albums most played by disc jockeys” and it was on that list of ten for about nine or ten months. It would be on at five and it would go to seven or eight, it would go back, it would go to two or three, it would go back to nine, and I’d think well that’s it, then it would go back to four, and back to six. It stayed on there for nine or ten months with airplay. But it really didn’t sell quite a bit until about six months. I mean it was negligible — fairly good sales, but after six months it was like your mom and dad or whoever were buying the records in those days, thought okay, somebody says, you can go buy it now if you want. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
They’d heard it so much, the airplay was wonderful. Finally they started going in and it became a gold record. And then we started following it up with a lot of others like it.
